heading: RAG II

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: RAG theory and learning path 01 Foundations: model knowledge, external sources, and the RAG workflow. 02 Retrieval: text units, representations, ranking, and candidate selection. 03 Generation: bounded context, claims, citations, and support review. 04 System design: evaluation, limitations, and research architectures. 05 Application: library objects and an optional implementation walkthrough. Lesson 04 — Learning path 02
heading: RAG theory and learning path

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) RAG adds selected external information to a language model’s input. Retrieval searches a collection for information relevant to a request. Augmentation adds selected retrieved content to the generator’s context. Generation produces a response conditioned on that context. Like an open-book response, the answer still needs accurate reading and support. Lesson 04 — 1. Foundations 03
heading: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Model memory and external sources Parametric memory Knowledge in learned model weights. Changing those weights usually requires further training. External memory A separate collection the system can search. Changes require refreshing affected source representations. RAG combines model knowledge with retrieved information during generation. Lesson 04 — 1. Foundations 04
heading: Model memory and external sources

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: RAG, fine-tuning, and long context Microsoft Foundry • Lewis et al. (2020) • Liu et al. (2024) 1 RAG Select external information for each request. The source collection and index can be refreshed. 2 Fine-tuning Train further to change model parameters. Adapt behavior, style, or task performance. 3 Long context Supply more material directly in the input. Input limits and effective use of that material still matter. These approaches affect different parts of a system and can be combined. Lesson 04 — 1. Foundations 05
heading: RAG, fine-tuning, and long context

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Index preparation and question answering Index preparation Acquire and parse sources. Create searchable passages. Build representations and an index. Preserve source information. Question-time processing Form the search query. Retrieve and select information. Construct the model context. Generate and review the response. Preparation creates the searchable collection that question answering uses. Lesson 04 — 1. Foundations 06
heading: Index preparation and question answering

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: The question-time RAG mechanism Query information need Retrieve candidate passages Select usable evidence Generate response draft Review claim support Respond answer or abstain Each stage transforms an input into the information needed by the next stage. Lesson 04 — 1. Foundations 07
heading: The question-time RAG mechanism

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Queries, documents, passages, and context These objects have different roles in the mechanism. Query q: a request expressing an information need. Document: a source item in a collection, such as a report or reference. Passage c: a source segment treated as a searchable unit. Context: everything the generator receives, including the query and selected evidence E. Lesson 04 — 1. Foundations 08
heading: Queries, documents, passages, and context

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Source ingestion, parsing, and metadata Search depends on readable content and preserved structure. Ingestion acquires content from the source collection. Parsing extracts text and structure, including headings and table relationships. Segmentation divides that content into searchable units. Metadata preserves descriptive information such as origin, date, section, and version. Lesson 04 — 2. Source preparation 09
heading: Source ingestion, parsing, and metadata

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Passage size and overlap LlamaIndex docs • LangChain docs 1 Small passages Offer precise matching. A split can remove a qualification or the information needed to interpret a fact. 2 Coherent passages Keep related statements and their conditions together. Meaning guides the boundary choice. 3 Large passages Preserve more surrounding text. Unrelated content can weaken matching and use context space. Overlap repeats boundary text to reduce split loss, while adding duplicate content. Lesson 04 — 2. Source preparation 10
heading: Passage size and overlap

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Provenance and source traceability Evidence must remain connected to its origin. Provenance records where information came from and how the system prepared it. Source identity distinguishes one reference from another. Version information identifies which source text the system used. A recoverable location points back to the supporting passage, page, or section. Lesson 04 — 2. Source preparation 11
heading: Provenance and source traceability

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Embeddings and dense representations Dense retrieval compares learned representations of text. An embedding maps text to a vector of numerical features. A query encoder represents the information need as a vector. A passage encoder represents source segments in a compatible space. A similarity function scores query–passage pairs for ranking. Lesson 04 — 2. Source preparation 12
heading: Embeddings and dense representations

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Cosine similarity and ranking Score definition cos(u, v) = (u · v) / (‖u‖ ‖v‖) u, v: nonzero query and passage vectors u · v: dot product ‖u‖, ‖v‖: vector lengths Interpretation Cosine compares vector direction. Unit vectors have length 1; their dot product equals cosine. Scores reflect the chosen text representation. A similarity score helps rank candidates. Source text establishes claim support. Lesson 04 — 3. Retrieval 13
heading: Cosine similarity and ranking

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Vector indexes and search constraints The index makes similarity search efficient at collection scale. A vector index organizes representations for searching. Exact search finds the best matches under the chosen metric. Approximate nearest-neighbor search trades exhaustive accuracy for efficiency. Filters restrict eligible candidates by source attributes or access rules. Lesson 04 — 3. Retrieval 14
heading: Vector indexes and search constraints

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Lexical, dense, and hybrid retrieval Qdrant docs • Elasticsearch docs • LlamaIndex docs 1 Lexical retrieval Ranks passages using weighted term matches. BM25 is a common lexical ranking method. 2 Dense retrieval Ranks passages through learned vector similarity. It can relate different wording when the representation captures that relation. 3 Hybrid retrieval Combines lexical and dense ranking signals. Fusion or reranking produces a candidate order. Retrieval methods differ in how they estimate relevance to the information need. Lesson 04 — 3. Retrieval 15
heading: Lexical, dense, and hybrid retrieval

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Query formulation and rewriting Search depends on how the information need is expressed. Query formulation turns the user’s request into a search input. Rewriting restores needed context or clarifies wording while preserving intent. Multiple queries explore complementary expressions of the same information need. Merged results need duplicate removal and evaluation against the original request. Lesson 04 — 3. Retrieval 16
heading: Query formulation and rewriting

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Candidate set and selected evidence Candidate set R Retrieval returns a ranked pool of potentially relevant passages. A broader pool can increase coverage and processing cost. Evidence set E Selection keeps the information the generator can use. E is a subset of R, constrained by usefulness and context space. Retrieval depth controls the search pool. Context depth controls the selected evidence. Lesson 04 — 3. Retrieval 17
heading: Candidate set and selected evidence

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Retrieval and reranking Efficient search narrows the pool before a more detailed relevance assessment. A bi-encoder represents queries and passages separately for efficient comparison. A cross-encoder examines a query and passage together to score their relationship. Reranking changes the order of a limited candidate set. Selection then chooses usable evidence. A relevance score still needs support review. Lesson 04 — 3. Retrieval 18
heading: Retrieval and reranking

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Evidence selection and context construction The candidate list becomes the generator’s available evidence. Selection keeps passages useful for answering the information need. Deduplication removes repeated content while preserving source identity. Context construction keeps source information attached to the selected text. The selection must preserve needed facts and conditions within the available budget. Lesson 04 — 3. Retrieval 19
heading: Evidence selection and context construction

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Context windows and token budgets The generator has limited space for reading and writing. A token is a model-specific text unit used for encoding and generation. The usable context window limits the sequence the model can process. Reserve space for instructions, history, the question, and generated output. Instructions + history + question + evidence + answer allowance ≤ window limit. Lesson 04 — 3. Retrieval 20
heading: Context windows and token budgets

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Retrieval checklist ☐ Source preparation preserves readable content, structure, and provenance. ☐ Representations and the search metric are compatible. ☐ The query, ranking method, candidate depth, and filters are declared. ☐ Retrieved passages contain information needed by the request. ☐ Selected evidence preserves meaning within the context budget. Lesson 04 — 3. Retrieval 21
heading: Retrieval checklist

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Generation conditioned on retrieved evidence P(y | q, E) The response depends on the question and selected evidence. q is the request, E is selected evidence, and y is the response. The prompt supplies instructions together with q and E. Generation predicts successive tokens using the available input and prior output. The response remains a draft until its claims are compared with the evidence. Lesson 04 — 4. Generation and grounding 22
heading: Generation conditioned on retrieved evidence

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Claims, evidence, and grounding Grounding is a relationship between an answer claim and supporting source content. Claim: one checkable factual statement in the response. Material claim: a statement whose truth affects the requested answer. Evidence: source content used to establish or challenge a claim. A grounded response gives identified support for its material claims. Lesson 04 — 4. Generation and grounding 23
heading: Claims, evidence, and grounding

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Supported, contradicted, or missing Compare each material claim with the available source content. Supported: the source establishes the claim and its relevant conditions. Contradicted: the source conflicts with the claim. Missing: the available evidence does not establish or contradict the claim. The complete response needs a review of every material claim. Lesson 04 — 4. Generation and grounding 24
heading: Supported, contradicted, or missing

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Citation and grounding Citation A pointer that lets the reader recover the source behind a claim. The pointer must resolve to the intended passage. Grounding A comparison between the claim and what the cited content establishes. The source must support the meaning and conditions of the claim. Attribution checks the source pointer. Support review checks the relationship to the claim. Lesson 04 — 4. Generation and grounding 25
heading: Citation and grounding

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Evidence sufficiency and abstention Question User’s information need Enough evidence? Needed facts and conditions are available. YES Answer generate and review a supported response NO Abstain State the missing information. Avoid unsupported details. Clarify an ambiguous request. Abstain when the available sources lack support. Lesson 04 — 4. Generation and grounding 26
heading: Evidence sufficiency and abstention

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: RAG failure types and repair priorities FAILED STAGE Retrieval Needed evidence is unavailable WHAT FAILS Generation Available evidence is misused REPAIR PRIORITY Attribution Source pointer is incorrect Inspect source coverage, search, and evidence selection. Inspect the draft’s meaning against the selected evidence. Inspect citation resolution and claim-to- source links. The earliest failed stage identifies which kind of repair to investigate. Lesson 04 — 4. Generation and grounding 27
heading: RAG failure types and repair priorities
headings: RAG failure types and repair priorities

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Inputs and outputs of the RAG mechanism Each output becomes the next stage’s input. Lesson 04 — 4. Generation and grounding 28 RETRIEVE Query q + source collection Output: ranked candidate set R SELECT Candidate set R + context budget Output: selected evidence E GENERATE Question q + evidence E Output: response draft y REVIEW Draft y + source evidence Output: support judgments and response decision
heading: Inputs and outputs of the RAG mechanism
headings: Inputs and outputs of the RAG mechanism

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Grounded response checklist ☐ Selected evidence preserves relevant facts and their conditions. ☐ Every material claim has identified supporting content. ☐ Every citation resolves to the intended source passage. ☐ Support review distinguishes agreement, conflict, and insufficient evidence. ☐ Clarification or abstention states the information gap when needed. Lesson 04 — 4. Generation and grounding 29
heading: Grounded response checklist

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Retrieval quality and response quality Retrieval evaluation Precision@k: relevant items in the top k, divided by k. Recall@k: relevant items found, divided by all labeled relevant items. Response evaluation Correctness: agreement with the reference facts. Grounding: support for material claims. Attribution: correct and sufficient source links. Lesson 04 — 5. Evaluation and limitations 30 Evaluate search and generation separately to locate the cause of a poor response.
heading: Retrieval quality and response quality

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Source freshness and RAG limitations OPERATING THE SYSTEM Reliable generation also depends on the quality of the available sources. Freshness requires detecting changes and refreshing affected representations. Conflicting sources require a policy for date, authority, and scope. Access rules determine which sources a request may use. Retrieved content can be incomplete or misleading, and the model can misread it. Lesson 04 — 5. Evaluation and limitations 31
heading: Source freshness and RAG limitations

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: RAG theory checklist ☐ Explain the roles of model parameters, external sources, and context. ☐ Distinguish candidate retrieval from evidence selection. ☐ Explain how the generator conditions on a query and selected evidence. ☐ Distinguish relevance, claim support, and citation correctness. ☐ Locate a failure by examining the first broken stage relationship. Lesson 04 — 5. Evaluation and limitations 32
heading: RAG theory checklist

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: RAG architecture choices LangChain docs • AI Engineering, Ch. 6 1 Fixed workflow Retrieval precedes generation through a declared sequence of stages. 2 Adaptive workflow The system decides when to search and may retrieve again as the request develops. 3 Modular design Query processing, search, selection, and review remain explicit components. Architecture determines when retrieval occurs and how information moves into generation. Lesson 04 — 6. Research architectures 33
heading: RAG architecture choices

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Original RAG: retrieval as latent evidence Lewis et al. • NeurIPS 2020 • arXiv:2005.11401 1 Model components A dense retriever weights candidate passages. A sequence-to-sequence generator conditions on each passage. 2 RAG-Sequence Each passage conditions a complete response. The model combines the alternatives using retrieval weights. 3 RAG-Token The model can combine passage-conditioned alternatives at each generated token. The original trained RAG model marginalizes over retrieved passages. Lesson 04 — 6. Research architectures 34
heading: Original RAG: retrieval as latent evidence
headings: Original RAG: retrieval as latent evidence

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Fusion-in-Decoder (FiD) Izacard & Grave • EACL 2021 • DOI:10.18653/v1/2021.eacl-main.74 1 Retrieve Retrieve several candidate passages relevant to the question. 2 Encode separately Encode each question-and- passage pair independently. 3 Fuse in decoding Let the decoder attend to the combined passage representations while generating. FiD combines retrieved information through the decoder’s attention. Lesson 04 — 6. Research architectures 35
heading: Fusion-in-Decoder (FiD)

title: RAG II Retrieval and Grounding
text: Active retrieval with FLARE Jiang et al. • EMNLP 2023 • DOI:10.18653/v1/2023.emnlp-main.495 1 Draft ahead Predict an upcoming sentence in the response. 2 Identify uncertainty Use low-confidence tokens to trigger an additional information search. 3 Retrieve and revise Retrieve relevant passages and regenerate the sentence using the new information. FLARE adapts retrieval to information needs that arise during generation. Lesson 04 — 6. Research architectures 36
heading: Active retrieval with FLARE

title: Improving RAG
text: Information need, relevance, and evidence DEFINITION A useful search result helps satisfy the user’s actual need. Information need: what the user wants to find out. Query: the words or representation sent to the search system. Relevance: how useful a passage is for that information need. Evidence sufficiency: whether the selected sources support the requested response. Lesson 05 — 1. Foundations 04
heading: Information need, relevance, and evidence

title: Improving RAG
text: The retrieval improvement workflow Request original need Rewrite search wording Filter eligible sources Retrieve candidate list Rerank new ordering Decide evidence suffices? preserve intent validate change enforce conditions retain sources retain identities proceed or abstain The decision concerns selected evidence. Generation and claim review follow. Lesson 05 — 1. Foundations 05
heading: The retrieval improvement workflow

title: Improving RAG
text: Four methods and their outputs REWRITE search wording a revised query clarify inspect output FILTER eligible sources a permitted subset restrict inspect output RERANK candidate order a ranked list compare inspect output GATE proceed decision a decision and reason assess inspect output Lesson 05 — 1. Foundations 06
heading: Four methods and their outputs

title: Improving RAG
text: Query rewriting DEFINITION Query rewriting changes how an information need is expressed for search. The original request remains the reference for meaning. The rewritten query makes useful search terms or context explicit. A rewrite may improve alignment with the collection’s wording. Validation checks that the transformation preserves the user’s constraints. Lesson 05 — 2. Query rewriting 07
heading: Query rewriting

title: Improving RAG
text: Query expansion and contextualization Query expansion • Add related search terms or normalize known terminology. • The information need stays the same. Contextualization • Restore context already established in the conversation. • Resolve references only when the context supports them. Both methods change search wording. Their validity depends on preserving intent. Lesson 05 — 2. Query rewriting 08
heading: Query expansion and contextualization

title: Improving RAG
text: Semantic drift and query invariants DEFINITION Semantic drift occurs when a rewrite changes the intended request. An invariant is a condition the transformation must preserve. Entities, dates, audiences, and negation can carry essential constraints. An added assumption can exclude relevant sources or change the task. A failed check triggers a declared fallback, clarification, or rejection. Lesson 05 — 2. Query rewriting 09
heading: Semantic drift and query invariants

title: Improving RAG
text: Example: a rewrite that preserves the request Lesson 05 — Visual example 10 Conversation context “I am an undergraduate. I need the 2026 laptop-loan policy.” User: “Can I keep one for a week?” Meaning preserved Can an undergraduate borrow a laptop for 7 days in 2026? One week becomes 7 days. Meaning changed Can a postgraduate borrow a laptop for 7 days in 2026? The audience changed without permission. Validation preserves audience, object, duration, and applicable policy year.
heading: Example: a rewrite that preserves the request
headings: Example: a rewrite that preserves the request

title: Improving RAG
text: Rewrite validation and fallback Validation • Compare the intended topic and every required constraint before retrieval. • Record unexplained additions and omissions. Fallback • Use the original request when it remains searchable. • Ask for clarification when the intended need is ambiguous. A fallback changes the search strategy while preserving mandatory constraints. Lesson 05 — 2. Query rewriting 11
heading: Rewrite validation and fallback

title: Improving RAG
text: Query rewriting summary 01 Keep the original request available for comparison. 02 Explain why the search wording needs to change. 03 Preserve required entities, dates, audience, and negation. 04 Identify every addition or omission that changes meaning. 05 Use a declared fallback when validation fails. Lesson 05 — 2. Query rewriting 12
heading: Query rewriting summary

title: Improving RAG
text: Metadata filtering DEFINITION A filter defines which source items are eligible for retrieval. Metadata describes source attributes beyond the passage text. A predicate is a condition that evaluates to true or false. Eligible items satisfy the required metadata conditions. Ranking then estimates relevance within the allowed search space. Lesson 05 — 3. Metadata filtering 13
heading: Metadata filtering

title: Improving RAG
text: Typed metadata and schema validity DEFINITION A metadata schema defines the attributes a system can interpret. A field has a declared meaning, value type, and allowed operations. Types distinguish text categories, numeric values, dates, and lists. Validation checks the requested condition against the stored representation. Missing, malformed, or stale metadata can change which sources retain. Lesson 05 — 3. Metadata filtering 14
heading: Typed metadata and schema validity

title: Improving RAG
text: Boolean logic in metadata filters DEFINITION A predicate can combine conditions using logical operators. AND requires every included condition to hold. OR requires at least one of the included conditions to hold. NOT excludes items that satisfy the specified condition. The combined predicate defines which source items are eligible. Lesson 05 — 3. Metadata filtering 15
heading: Boolean logic in metadata filters

title: Improving RAG
text: Example: filtering by audience and policy year Lesson 05 — Visual example 16 Required conditions: undergraduate audience AND policy year 2026 ID Audience Year Passage states Eligible? A Undergraduates 2026 Maximum continuous laptop loan: 3 days. Yes B Postgraduates 2026 Maximum continuous laptop loan: 7 days. No: audience C Undergraduates 2024 Maximum continuous laptop loan: 7 days. No: year D Undergraduates 2026 Library closes at 20:00. Yes A and D pass the filter. D still does not answer the laptop-loan question.
heading: Example: filtering by audience and policy year
headings: Example: filtering by audience and policy year

title: Improving RAG
text: Prefiltering and postfiltering Prefiltering • Apply eligibility conditions during candidate retrieval. • The search returns matches within the allowed subset. Postfiltering • Retrieve a limited candidate list, then remove ineligible items. • Eligible results outside that list remain unavailable. The same predicate can yield different results when it executes at a different stage. Lesson 05 — 3. Metadata filtering 17
heading: Prefiltering and postfiltering

title: Improving RAG
text: Example: why filter placement changes the pool Lesson 05 — Visual example 18 Same unfiltered order: B, C, D, A. Retrieval returns at most 2 items. POSTFILTER Retrieve "top 2" B, C Apply conditions B fails audience. C fails year. Empty pool A never entered the retrieved list. PREFILTER Filter A and D are eligible. Search subset D, A Evidence available A can enter later selection. A later filter cannot recover an eligible source missing from a limited pool.
heading: Example: why filter placement changes the pool
headings: Example: why filter placement changes the pool

title: Improving RAG
text: Empty results and candidate starvation DEFINITION An empty list describes the search outcome under the current conditions. No matching source may exist in the collection. Missing metadata or an incorrect predicate may exclude useful material. Limited retrieval followed by filtering may leave no surviving candidates. The response policy can clarify, abstain, or retry within the same mandatory rules. Lesson 05 — 3. Metadata filtering 19
heading: Empty results and candidate starvation

title: Improving RAG
text: Filtering summary 01 Ground each required condition in the request or application policy. 02 Validate field meaning, value type, and supported operations. 03 State whether filtering occurs during or after retrieval. 04 Inspect empty results and missing metadata explicitly. 05 Keep mandatory constraints active in every fallback. Lesson 05 — 3. Metadata filtering 20
heading: Filtering summary

title: Improving RAG
text: Candidate retrieval and reranking RETRIEVE search the collection produce candidates RERANK compare candidates produce a new order SELECT choose evidence respect the context budget candidate generation candidate ordering Reranking can only promote passages available in its input candidate set. Lesson 05 — 4. Ranking and decisions 21
heading: Candidate retrieval and reranking

title: Improving RAG
text: Pointwise, pairwise, and listwise ranking 1 Pointwise Assess one candidate’s relevance to the query at a time. 2 Pairwise Compare two candidates for the same query and predict their relative order. 3 Listwise Consider several candidates together and produce or optimize their ordering. The distinction concerns how candidates participate in the ranking decision. Lesson 05 — 4. Ranking and decisions 22
heading: Pointwise, pairwise, and listwise ranking

title: Improving RAG
text: Bi-encoders and cross-encoders Bi-encoder retrieval • Encode the query and each passage separately. • Prepared passage vectors support efficient similarity search. Cross-encoder reranking • Process the query and one candidate together. • Joint attention supports a more detailed relevance assessment. Two-stage search reserves the more expensive joint assessment for a smaller list. Lesson 05 — 4. Ranking and decisions 23
heading: Bi-encoders and cross-encoders

title: Improving RAG
text: Example: reranking changes order, not sources Lesson 05 — Visual example 24 Can an undergraduate borrow a laptop for 7 days in 2026? Initial candidate order After relevance reranking D Undergraduate hours guide Undergraduates, policy year 2026 The library closes at 20:00. A Undergraduate loan guide Undergraduates, policy year 2026 Maximum continuous laptop loan: 3 calendar days. A Undergraduate loan guide Undergraduates, policy year 2026 Maximum continuous laptop loan: 3 calendar days. D Undergraduate hours guide Undergraduates, policy year 2026 The library closes at 20:00. A addresses loan duration. D describes opening hours. The same two sources remain.

headings: Example: reranking changes order, not sources

title: Improving RAG
text: Ranking and the decision to proceed Ranking • Estimate relative relevance and order the candidate passages. • A first-place result can still be inadequate. Evidence decision • Assess selected evidence against the information needed to answer. • Proceed, clarify, retry, or abstain under a declared policy. Here the gate acts on a request’s selected evidence before generation. Lesson 05 — 4. Ranking and decisions 25
heading: Ranking and the decision to proceed
headings: Ranking and the decision to proceed

title: Improving RAG
text: Scores, ranks, and decision signals DEFINITION Each signal needs a defined interpretation. A retrieval score reflects a retriever’s matching function. A reranking score reflects a second assessment of candidate relevance. A rank is a position relative to other candidates in that list. A gate decision applies an application rule to available evidence signals. Lesson 05 — 4. Ranking and decisions 26
heading: Scores, ranks, and decision signals

title: Improving RAG
text: Evidence sufficiency and abstention DEFINITION Enough topical overlap does not guarantee enough information to answer. Sufficiency concerns the facts and conditions the response requires. Missing or conflicting evidence can prevent a supported response. Abstention reports that the current evidence cannot support an answer. Threshold calibration requires labeled evaluation beyond this lesson. Lesson 05 — 4. Ranking and decisions 27
heading: Evidence sufficiency and abstention

title: Improving RAG
text: Example: enough evidence can support “No” Lesson 05 — Visual example 28 Can an undergraduate borrow a laptop for 7 days in 2026? Same request and source collection. Only the selected evidence differs. Selected evidence Decision Response A Undergraduate loan guide Undergraduates, policy year 2026 Maximum continuous laptop loan: 3 calendar days. Proceed The loan rule is available. No. The maximum continuous loan is 3 days. D Undergraduate hours guide Undergraduates, policy year 2026 The library closes at 20:00. Abstain Loan duration is missing. The selected evidence cannot answer this request. Sufficiency supports an answer, including “No”. A pass still needs claim review.
heading: Example: enough evidence can support “No”

title: Improving RAG
text: Candidate sets, ordering, and selected evidence Eligible allowed sources Retrieved candidate pool Reranked same identities Selected evidence subset Decision proceed or abstain Eligibility restricts membership. Reranking orders. Selection chooses evidence. The sufficiency decision considers the selected evidence for the request. Lesson 05 — 4. Ranking and decisions 29

headings: Candidate sets, ordering, and selected evidence

title: Improving RAG
text: Ranking and evidence summary 01 Separate candidate generation, ordering, and evidence selection. 02 Define the origin and meaning of each score. 03 State whether a decision applies to one passage or the whole request. 04 Record why the evidence permits proceeding or requires abstention. 05 Review generated claims even after a pre-generation pass. Lesson 05 — 4. Ranking and decisions 30
heading: Ranking and evidence summary

heading: Execution cost and latency

title: Improving RAG
text: Intervention provenance and rollback DEFINITION A trace records how a request reached its result. Provenance identifies inputs, component versions, and applied policies. Intermediate outputs show where candidate membership or order changed. A regression is a case that becomes worse under the new method. Rollback restores a prior valid method when the change is unjustified. Lesson 05 — 5. Controlled improvement 32
heading: Intervention provenance and rollback

title: Improving RAG
text: Levels of observation in an improvement study REQUEST: intended need and required constraints TRANSFORMATION: search wording and eligibility conditions CANDIDATES: membership, order, and signal origins DECISION: selected evidence, outcome, and rationale COMPARISON: changed behavior, regressions, and cost Records connect each outcome to the stage that changed it. headings: Levels of observation in an improvement study

title: Improving RAG
text: Baseline and controlled comparison DEFINITION A baseline is the reference system used to assess a change. A control is a condition kept fixed across the comparison. An intervention is the component or policy intentionally changed. Use the same requests, collection revision, and compatible representations. Compare intermediate outputs, outcomes, regressions, and execution cost. Lesson 05 — 5. Controlled improvement 34
heading: Baseline and controlled comparison

title: Improving RAG
text: Paired comparisons and ablations Paired comparison Run two configurations on the same requests. Several components may differ, so the result reflects their combined change. Ablation Remove or vary one component while holding the others fixed. This isolates that component’s contribution in the tested setting. A paired demonstration becomes a causal attribution claim only with adequate controls. Lesson 05 — 5. Controlled improvement 35
heading: Paired comparisons and ablations

title: Improving RAG
text: Example: a controlled reranking comparison Lesson 05 — Visual example 36 Held fixed Same query, sources, and pool D, A. Select the first item and use the same evidence rule. Reranking OFF Candidate order D first, then A Selected D hours guide Outcome Insufficient loan evidence Reranking ON Candidate order A first, then D Selected A loan guide Outcome Enough evidence to answer No Only reranking changes. Selection and decision outcomes follow from that change.
heading: Example: a controlled reranking comparison

title: Improving RAG
text: Regressions and improvement claims DEFINITION An improvement needs evidence across the intended use cases. Declare the desired behavior before inspecting the changed result. Examine cases that improve, worsen, or stay unchanged. Check whether extra cost and exclusions are acceptable. Use representative labeled evaluation before claiming general effectiveness. Lesson 05 — 5. Controlled improvement 37

heading: Method benefits, costs, and limitations

title: Improving RAG
text: Mechanism summary 01 Explain which object each method changes. 02 Distinguish eligibility, relevance, and evidence sufficiency. 03 Keep ranking separate from evidence selection and final support review. 04 Identify a fair baseline and the intervention under comparison. 05 Limit every improvement claim to the evidence actually collected. title: Improving RAG
text: Rewrite–Retrieve–Read 1 Rewrite Turn the information request into search queries suited to the retriever. 2 Retrieve Search with those queries and collect source passages. 3 Read Use the request and retrieved passages to produce a response. Ma et al. place query adaptation before search. Lesson 05 — 6. Research mechanisms 40
heading: Rewrite–Retrieve–Read

title: Improving RAG
text: Prompted and learned query rewriting 1 Prompted method A fixed language model follows instructions to produce search wording. 2 Learned method A separate rewriter adapts using feedback from the downstream task. 3 Objective Optimize useful retrieval and task outcomes, beyond the rewrite’s fluency. The component that adapts is the rewriter. Search and reading can remain fixed. Lesson 05 — 6. Research mechanisms 41
heading: Prompted and learned query rewriting

title: Improving RAG
text: Hypothetical Document Embeddings (HyDE) 1 Generate Generate document-like text for the information need. 2 Encode Encode that text in the same space as the indexed documents. 3 Retrieve Search for real corpus documents near the resulting representation. HyDE uses hypothetical text to construct a search representation. Lesson 05 — 6. Research mechanisms 42
heading: Hypothetical Document Embeddings (HyDE)

title: Improving RAG
text: Hypothetical text and retrieved evidence 1 Representation Document-like wording can reduce the mismatch between a short query and passages. 2 Source evidence Real retrieved documents supply the source material used for answering. 3 Limitation Generated details can be false and can steer search toward the wrong material. A generated search representation does not establish the truth of its contents. Lesson 05 — 6. Research mechanisms 43
